sections.title: When money is cheaper than wallpaper
sections.intro_md:
In the autumn of 1923 Germans pasted banknotes on their walls as wallpaper, because the paper was worth more than the money. A loaf of bread in Berlin that cost about **160 marks** at the end of 1922 cost about **200 billion marks** by late 1923.

Eighty-five years later, in Harare, the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe printed a note for **100 trillion dollars**. Ten years after that, in Caracas, a Reuters photographer laid a 2.4 kg chicken next to the pile of cash needed to buy it: **14.6 million bolivars**, about two US dollars.

Three continents, nearly a century apart, one disease. Today is about how money dies: what the word hyperinflation really means, why it happens, what it does to ordinary people, how it ends, and why it keeps coming back. And about the strange objects it leaves behind.

spotlights.name: Wallpapering with marks, 1923
spotlights.spot_it: A black and white photo of a man pasting real banknotes onto a wall, row after row.
spotlights.story_md: This is one of the most reproduced photos of the German inflation, kept in the Bundesarchiv, the German federal archive. It shows banknotes used as wallpaper. By late 1923 the Reichsbank's printing contractors could not keep up, and old low-denomination notes were overprinted, bundled and weighed rather than counted. The Deutsches Historisches Museum notes that at the end, the first inflation notes were worth more as paper than as money, so people overprinted them as tickets, receipts and greeting cards.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the image most people carry in their heads when they hear the word hyperinflation.
spotlights.memory_hook: When the money is worth less than the paper, the money becomes the wallpaper.

spotlights.name: The Z$100 trillion note
spotlights.spot_it: A blue-green note with the Chiremba balancing rocks and fourteen digits: 100,000,000,000,000.
spotlights.story_md: Zimbabwe issued its 100 trillion dollar note on **16 January 2009**, with $10, $20 and $50 trillion notes in the same month. It is the banknote that shows the most zeros ever printed in full, fourteen of them. Three weeks later the government cut twelve zeros, and by April 2009 it abandoned its own currency for US dollars and South African rand. In 2015 the central bank offered to buy old notes back at about 40 US cents for 100 trillion. By then collectors were paying far more: tens of dollars online, and dealers in 2026 list crisp uncirculated notes near 200 dollars. It is one of the few notes worth more dead than alive.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The most famous object of 21st century hyperinflation, and a reminder that it can happen in a modern economy with ATMs and mobile phones.
spotlights.memory_hook: Fourteen zeros, three weeks of life, now a souvenir.

sections.title: What counts as hyperinflation
sections.intro_md:
Ordinary inflation is prices creeping up. India's central bank aims for **4 percent a year**. High inflation is 20, 50, even 100 percent a year: painful, but people still use the money.

**Hyperinflation** is different in kind. The standard line was drawn in 1956 by the American economist **Phillip Cagan**: prices rising **more than 50 percent in a single month**. Kept up for a year, that compounds to roughly **13,000 percent**, prices multiplying about 130 times. An episode ends when monthly inflation falls below 50 percent and stays there for a year.

The best scorecard is the **Hanke-Krus World Hyperinflation Table** (Cato Institute, 2012), which listed **56** episodes; Venezuela became the 57th in December 2016. Almost all happened in the 20th century, after paper money cut loose from gold. The single best number for feeling the speed is the **doubling time**: how long until prices double. In Hungary in July 1946 it was about **15 hours**.

spotlights.name: Cagan's 50 percent rule
spotlights.spot_it: A single line on a chart: 50 percent price rise in one month.
spotlights.story_md: Phillip Cagan, then a young economist at the University of Chicago working with Milton Friedman, wrote *The Monetary Dynamics of Hyperinflation* in 1956, the first serious modern study of the subject. He needed a clean definition, so he picked one: an episode starts in the month prices rise more than 50 percent, and ends when monthly inflation falls below 50 percent and stays there for at least a year. The number is arbitrary, but it stuck because it captures a real change in behaviour. Below it, people still hold the money for a while. Above it, everyone tries to get rid of cash the moment it arrives, and that rush is what turns high inflation into collapse.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Every count of hyperinflations, including today's three countries, uses Cagan's line.
spotlights.memory_hook: Fifty in a month, and money turns into a hot potato.

spotlights.name: Doubling time
spotlights.spot_it: A price tag that has to be rewritten before lunch.
spotlights.story_md: Percentages stop meaning anything at these speeds: 79.6 billion percent a month is just noise. Economists therefore translate the rate into how long it takes for prices to double. At Zimbabwe's November 2008 peak that was **24.7 hours**, so a loaf of bread cost about twice as much each morning. In Hungary in July 1946 it was about **15 hours**, so prices doubled between breakfast and dinner. In Germany at the October 1923 peak it was about **3.7 days**. Venezuela's worst months in 2018 doubled prices in roughly two to three weeks. The logarithmic chart shown here plots the German price level from 1914 to 1923; on a normal scale the line would be flat for years and then vanish off the top of the page.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the one number that lets you feel the speed.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ask not what percent, ask how many hours.

sections.title: How a currency dies
sections.intro_md:
The recipe has been almost the same every time. Peter Bernholz studied 29 hyperinflations and found that at least 25 began the same way: **a government spends far more than it collects in taxes and covers the gap by having the central bank create money.**

Stage one: the deficit. A war, reparations, an oil crash or a collapse in farm output leaves a hole in the budget. Stage two: printing. The central bank buys government debt with new money. Prices rise, but slowly, because people still trust the money. Stage three: **expectations flip**. Once people expect tomorrow's prices to be higher, they spend wages the day they get them. Money changes hands faster and faster, so prices rise faster than the printing presses. Stage four: tax revenue collapses, because taxes are paid weeks after they are assessed, in money that has since melted (the Olivera-Tanzi effect). So the state prints more. Stage five: people abandon the currency for dollars, gold, cigarettes or barter. Economists call this Thiers' law: in a collapse, good money drives out bad.

No country chooses hyperinflation. It gets there by deciding, again and again, that printing is less painful today than cutting spending or raising taxes.

spotlights.name: The inflation tax
spotlights.spot_it: No law, no form, no tax office: your savings simply buy less each week.
spotlights.story_md: When a government pays its bills with new money, it takes real goods from everyone who holds the old money. Economists call this **seigniorage** or the inflation tax. It is attractive because no parliament votes for it. But it has a trap. The faster prices rise, the less cash people are willing to hold, so the tax base shrinks. Beyond a point, printing more brings in less real revenue, not more. Cagan showed that the hyperinflating governments he studied printed past that point. The Weimar state also enjoyed a hidden gift: its domestic war debt, about **164 billion marks**, was worth just **16.4 pfennig** by the currency reform of November 1923.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It explains why governments start printing, and why printing more eventually fails.
spotlights.memory_hook: The tax nobody votes for, until there is nothing left to tax.

spotlights.name: The hot potato: velocity explodes
spotlights.spot_it: Workers running from the factory gate to the shop with their pay in a sack.
spotlights.story_md: The quantity theory of money says prices depend not just on how much money exists but on how fast it is spent. In normal times a rupee or a dollar might change hands a few times a month. In hyperinflation people pass money on like a hot potato. German workers in 1923 were often paid daily, sometimes twice a day, and wives waited at the gates to rush the cash to the shops before the next exchange rate was posted. Shops in turn set their opening hours by the times new dollar rates were announced. Because velocity rises, prices race ahead of the printing presses, and the paradox follows: in the middle of a flood of money, there is a **shortage of cash**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is why hyperinflation feels like a cash shortage, not a cash glut.
spotlights.memory_hook: Too much money, never enough notes.

sections.title: Before Weimar: paper promises
sections.intro_md:
Hyperinflation needs paper. Coins can be debased only so fast; paper has no such limit. The two great early experiments came out of revolutions.

The American colonies fought Britain with **Continental dollars**, bills of credit printed by the Continental Congress from 1775. By 1780 they were worth about one-fortieth of face value; 'not worth a Continental' became an American idiom, and the shock is why the US Constitution later barred states from making anything but gold and silver coin legal tender. Revolutionary France printed **assignats** from 1789, at first backed by land seized from the Church. By 1796 issues had reached tens of billions of livres, and France's 1795-96 episode is the oldest entry in the Hanke-Krus table.

spotlights.name: The Continental dollar
spotlights.spot_it: Small hand-sized notes with Latin mottoes and leaf prints, signed by hand.
spotlights.story_md: To fight the War of Independence, the Continental Congress printed paper bills of credit, promising redemption in coin at some future date. Benjamin Franklin designed some of them and used real leaf prints to make them hard to forge. Congress and the states printed far more than they could ever redeem, and the British forged them on purpose to speed the collapse. By 1780 a Continental bill was worth about one-fortieth of its face value. The phrase 'not worth a Continental' survives in American English. The memory was so bitter that the 1787 Constitution forbade the states to issue bills of credit or make anything but gold and silver coin legal tender.
spotlights.why_it_matters: America's founding inflation shaped its constitution and its suspicion of paper money.
spotlights.memory_hook: 'Not worth a Continental' was once a precise exchange rate.

spotlights.name: The French assignat
spotlights.spot_it: A small paper note with revolutionary symbols, the Phrygian cap and 'Republique francaise'.
spotlights.story_md: In December 1789 the bankrupt revolutionary state voted to issue assignats, interest-bearing certificates secured on the vast lands confiscated from the Catholic Church. They soon became ordinary paper money. War with Europe from 1792 multiplied the printing, the government tried price controls and forced acceptance at par, and forgeries poured in. By 1796 the issue had reached about 45 billion livres and the notes were nearly worthless. France replaced them with a new paper, the mandat territorial, which failed even faster. France's 1795-96 collapse is the only episode older than the 20th century in the Hanke-Krus table.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The first modern state to print its way through a revolution and a war, and the template for many later ones.
spotlights.memory_hook: Backed by church land, killed by war.

sections.title: Weimar: the road to 1923
sections.intro_md:
Germany went to war in 1914 planning to pay for it with victory. Unlike France and Britain, it raised taxes very little and borrowed instead: of about **164 billion marks** of war costs, only about 10 billion came from taxes. The mark slipped from **4.2 to the dollar** in 1914 to 7.9 by 1918.

The new republic inherited the debt, pensions for millions of war victims and, from May 1921, the **London Schedule of Payments**: reparations of 132 billion gold marks on paper, of which about 50 billion were expected in practice. Budgets never balanced. The **Reichsbank** under **Rudolf Havenstein** kept discounting Treasury bills, which meant printing.

After the foreign minister **Walther Rathenau** was murdered in June 1922, confidence broke. The mark went from about **320 per dollar** in mid-1922 to **7,400** in December. In January 1923 French and Belgian troops **occupied the Ruhr** to collect coal in kind. Berlin ordered passive resistance and paid the striking workers with freshly printed money. By November 1923 one dollar bought **4,210,500,000,000 marks**.

spotlights.name: Rudolf Havenstein
spotlights.spot_it: An elderly official with a white beard and pince-nez, the face behind the German printing presses.
spotlights.story_md: Rudolf Havenstein ran the Reichsbank from 1908 until his death on 20 November 1923, five days after the new Rentenmark appeared. He was a conscientious Prussian civil servant who saw his job as supplying the economy with the money it demanded. When prices rose, businesses needed more notes, so he printed more notes. In 1923 he spoke proudly to the Reichstag of how much new money his presses could now turn out. The British ambassador Lord D'Abernon wrote that no dog had ever chased its own tail with the speed of the Reichsbank. A 1915 caricature from the war-loan years already called him 'General Geldmarschall', the field marshal of money.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He shows that hyperinflation can be run by careful, honest people with the wrong theory.
spotlights.memory_hook: The man who printed to meet demand, and found demand had no ceiling.

spotlights.name: The occupation of the Ruhr
spotlights.spot_it: French soldiers with rifles standing guard over coal yards and railway lines in Essen.
spotlights.story_md: After Germany defaulted on coal deliveries for the 34th time in 36 months, French and Belgian troops marched into the Ruhr, Germany's industrial heart, on 11 January 1923. The government of Wilhelm Cuno answered with **passive resistance**: miners, railwaymen and officials refused to work for the occupiers. The strike was patriotic and ruinous. The Reich lost the Ruhr's output and taxes and still had to pay millions of idle workers, so it printed the money. This is the point where German inflation turned into hyperinflation. Gustav Stresemann called off the resistance in September 1923; the French and Belgians collected about 900 million gold marks this way and left by August 1925.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the trigger that turned a bad inflation into the famous one.
spotlights.memory_hook: Pay a nation not to work, with money from a printing press.

spotlights.name: 133 printing works, 1,783 presses
spotlights.spot_it: Clerks in a Berlin bank surrounded by bundles and baskets of notes.
spotlights.story_md: The state printer, the Reichsdruckerei, could not keep up. By autumn 1923 up to **133 outside firms** with **1,783 printing presses** were working for it day and night. According to the Deutsches Historisches Museum, **30 paper mills** made the banknote paper, 29 electroplating workshops made about 400,000 printing plates, and around **30,000 people** produced roughly **10 billion** notes. The top denomination reached 100 trillion marks in November 1923. It still was not enough: more than **5,800** towns, counties and companies printed their own emergency money. In banks, notes were bundled and moved in laundry baskets; this Library of Congress photo, 'In a Berlin bank', shows the scene.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The industrial scale of it is the point: this was a national factory producing worthlessness.
spotlights.memory_hook: Thirty thousand people working round the clock to make money worth nothing.

sections.title: Living through 1923
sections.intro_md:
Daily life in 1923, as the Deutsches Historisches Museum records it: wages were often paid **daily**. Shops set opening hours by the moment new exchange rates were announced. In restaurants the bill could **double during the meal**, so diners paid when they ordered. Pastors held out laundry baskets for the Sunday collection. Thieves stopped bothering with wallets and went for valuables, even gold teeth. Real wages fell to about **40 percent** of pre-war.

Who lost? Anyone with savings, a pension or war bonds: the middle class that had lent the Kaiser its money. Who won? Debtors, above all the state, because 'a mark is a mark': a debt of 1,000 pre-war marks could legally be settled with 1,000 marks of 1923.

spotlights.name: Notgeld: emergency money
spotlights.spot_it: Local notes from towns and firms, often colourful, with city crests, local heroes, jokes and dialect verses.
spotlights.story_md: When the Reichsbank could not print fast enough, towns, districts, savings banks and companies printed their own money, known as **Notgeld**. More than 5,800 issuers did so in 1923 alone, and the DHM estimates that over 700 quintillion marks of Notgeld were issued, more than the Reichsbank's own 524 quintillion. Some were crude stamps; others were small works of art, like this ten-million-mark note from Trier designed by Fritz Quant. In late 1923 some issuers switched to 'stable value' notes denominated in rye, wheat, coal, timber, sugar, bacon or gas. Collectors were already buying Notgeld in the early 1920s, and some towns printed series purely to sell to them.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how money splinters when the centre fails, and how much design people poured into it.
spotlights.memory_hook: When the Reich could not print enough, every town became a mint.

spotlights.name: Herbert Bayer's Bauhaus banknotes
spotlights.spot_it: A red one-million-mark note with no eagle, no hero, no crest: just big sans-serif numerals and blocks of colour.
spotlights.story_md: In August 1923 the State Bank of Thuringia commissioned emergency notes from the Bauhaus in Weimar, and the young typographer **Herbert Bayer**, then a student there, designed them in days. He threw out the old banknote vocabulary of coats of arms and portraits. His notes use bold sans-serif type, asymmetric layout and flat primary colours, and the print colour changed every few days through the run. The V&A in London holds a red one-million-mark note. They had almost no purchasing power, yet they are now classics of modern graphic design. Bayer later emigrated to the United States and became one of the most influential designers of the century.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The most worthless money of 1923 became one of the most valued pieces of Bauhaus design.
spotlights.memory_hook: A million marks that bought almost nothing and taught designers everything.

spotlights.name: Overprinted notes: a thousand becomes a billion
spotlights.spot_it: An ordinary 1,000-mark note with a big red stamp across it reading 'Eine Milliarde Mark'.
spotlights.story_md: Designing and printing new notes took weeks; prices doubled in days. So the Reichsbank took stocks of existing notes and stamped new values over them. This 1,000-mark Reichsbank note of December 1922 was overprinted in 1923 to read **one billion marks**, a millionfold promotion with a rubber stamp. Postage stamps went the same way, overprinted with Tausend, Millionen and Milliarden. By November 1923 the highest note was 100 trillion marks, printed on one side only to save time and ink.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It captures the speed: there was no time even to design the money.
spotlights.memory_hook: A rubber stamp could make a note a million times richer, and the note still bought less.

spotlights.name: Hugo Stinnes, the inflation king
spotlights.spot_it: A dark-bearded industrialist in a plain suit, the richest and most hated businessman of 1923 Germany.
spotlights.story_md: Hugo Stinnes was already a coal and shipping magnate before 1914. During the inflation he borrowed heavily in paper marks and bought on a vast scale: mines, steelworks, shipping lines, hotels, newspapers and paper mills. Because 'a mark is a mark', he repaid the loans in money that had lost almost all its value, while his assets were real. The DHM names him as the classic winner of the inflation. He died in April 1924, months after the currency was stabilised, and the empire fell apart within a few years under its debts in stable money.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He shows who gains in hyperinflation: debtors with real assets.
spotlights.memory_hook: Borrow in melting money, buy in steel.

sections.title: How Germany stopped it
sections.intro_md:
The German hyperinflation ended astonishingly fast. In August 1923 **Gustav Stresemann** became chancellor and in September called off the Ruhr resistance. On 15 October a new bank, the **Rentenbank**, was founded, and on **15 November 1923** it issued the **Rentenmark**. One Rentenmark was set equal to **one trillion paper marks**, so 4.2 Rentenmarks bought a dollar, the exact pre-war rate.

The new money had no gold behind it. It was nominally secured on a mortgage on Germany's farmland and industry, which nobody could actually redeem. What made it work was a hard limit on its quantity and a promise that the government would not borrow it: on 12 November **Hjalmar Schacht** became currency commissioner, and the Reichsbank stopped discounting Treasury bills. The budget was balanced by January 1924 with deep cuts. The **Dawes Plan** of 1924 rescheduled reparations, and in August the **Reichsmark** replaced both currencies. A 1925 law restored old mortgages at 25 percent of their value, too little for ruined savers.

spotlights.name: The Rentenmark
spotlights.spot_it: Plain notes headed 'Rentenbankschein', dated 1 November 1923, with no portrait at all.
spotlights.story_md: The Rentenmark was a confidence trick in the best sense. Its legal backing was a mortgage charged on German agricultural and industrial land, and Rentenmarks could be swapped for interest-bearing bonds indexed to gold, but not for gold itself. What mattered was the quantity: just 500 million Rentenmarks were in circulation by 30 November 1923, 1.8 billion by July 1924. The old paper marks kept circulating alongside, and went on growing to 1.2 sextillion, but prices quoted in the new money stayed still. Twelve zeros were simply struck off price tags. Germans soon called the episode the 'miracle of the Rentenmark'.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Proof that belief, backed by real limits, can restore money in weeks.
spotlights.memory_hook: One new mark for a trillion old ones, and prices stood still.

spotlights.name: Hjalmar Schacht
spotlights.spot_it: A tall, stiff banker with a very high starched collar and round glasses.
spotlights.story_md: Hjalmar Schacht was a Berlin banker appointed currency commissioner on 12 November 1923, and Reichsbank president after Havenstein died on 20 November. His central decision was to refuse: no more discounting of government bills, no credit for speculators, and a strict cap on the new money. He became a hero of sound money, and later a much darker figure: he served Hitler as Reichsbank president and economics minister in the 1930s, financing rearmament, and was tried and acquitted at Nuremberg in 1946.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The banker who ended the inflation, and whose later career is a warning of its own.
spotlights.memory_hook: The man who said no, and later said yes to the wrong people.

sections.title: The record holders
sections.intro_md:
Weimar is the most famous hyperinflation, but not the worst. The Hanke-Krus table ranks it fifth. The top of the list belongs to wars and occupations.

**Hungary, 1945-46**, holds the world record. After the war and Soviet occupation, with factories stripped and reparations owed, prices peaked in July 1946 at about **41.9 quadrillion percent a month**: doubling roughly every **15 hours**. When the forint replaced the pengo in August 1946, all Hungarian notes in circulation were worth about a thousandth of a US cent.

**Yugoslavia, 1992-94**, under UN sanctions and at war, cut zeros again and again until in January 1994 a new dinar was tied one-to-one to the Deutsche Mark. **Greece** under German and Italian occupation hit 13,800 percent in a single month in October 1944, as occupiers made the Bank of Greece print drachmas to buy Greek goods. **China's** Nationalist government lost the civil war partly to its gold yuan, launched in 1948 and dead within a year.

spotlights.name: The b-pengo notes of 1946
spotlights.spot_it: Hungarian notes of 1946 with the number spelled out in words, such as 'milliard b.-pengo', rather than in digits.
spotlights.story_md: Hungary's 1946 notes ran out of room for zeros, so they used words. 'B-pengo' meant billion-pengo, a million million. The **100 million b-pengo** note, 10 to the power 20 pengo, is the highest denomination ever issued for circulation. A note for a billion b-pengo, ten times larger, was printed but never issued. To keep taxes alive, the state created the **adopengo**, a tax unit whose value was announced daily by radio; by late July one adopengo was worth 2 sextillion pengo. When the forint arrived in August 1946, one forint replaced 400 octillion (4 followed by 29 zeros) pengo. The note shown here is that unissued one sextillion pengo note. Zimbabwe's 100 trillion note shows more zeros, but the pengo notes were far larger.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The biggest number ever printed on money meant for spending.
spotlights.memory_hook: Too many zeros to print, so they wrote it in words.

spotlights.name: Yugoslavia's 1993 dinar notes
spotlights.spot_it: Notes of 1993 with ever more zeros: 5,000, then 50 million, 500 million, and finally 500 billion dinars.
spotlights.story_md: The breakup of Yugoslavia, war in Bosnia and UN sanctions from 1992 wrecked the economy of the rump Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (Serbia and Montenegro). The state printed to pay soldiers, pensions and loss-making firms. Monthly inflation was projected at a million percent by December 1993. Currency reforms struck off 1 zero, then 6, then 9. Notes went from thousands to millions to a 500 billion dinar note by the end of 1993. In January 1994 the central bank governor **Dragoslav Avramovic** launched a new dinar pegged one-to-one to the Deutsche Mark and backed by reserves. Inflation stopped almost at once, and Avramovic became a folk hero.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Europe's most recent hyperinflation, ended by tying the currency to a stable one.
spotlights.memory_hook: Half a trillion dinars, then one dinar equals one Deutsche Mark.

sections.title: Zimbabwe: from breadbasket to bearer cheques
sections.intro_md:
At independence in 1980 the Zimbabwe dollar was worth more than a US dollar at the official rate. The country fed itself and exported maize, beef and above all tobacco. The slide began in the late 1990s: unbudgeted payouts to independence war veterans in 1997, then an expensive military intervention in the Congo war from 1998.

The decisive blow came in **2000**, when President **Robert Mugabe's** government launched 'fast-track' land reform, seizing most of the roughly 4,000 large commercial farms, mostly white-owned, often violently, and handing them to new farmers, many with no capital or experience and some of them political allies. Output collapsed. Tobacco, the biggest export earner, fell from about **237 million kg in 2000** to under **50 million kg in 2008**. With exports, taxes and foreign credit drying up, the Reserve Bank under **Gideon Gono** (governor from December 2003) printed money to fund the state, loss-making parastatals and its own farm-mechanisation and subsidy schemes.

In mid-2007 the government ordered shops to halve prices; shelves emptied within weeks, because nobody would produce at a loss.

spotlights.name: Robert Mugabe
spotlights.spot_it: An elderly man in thick-rimmed glasses and a small square moustache, often in a bright party-print shirt or a dark suit.
spotlights.story_md: Robert Mugabe led Zimbabwe from independence in 1980 until a military takeover forced him out in November 2017; he died in 2019. A former teacher and guerrilla leader, he was first praised abroad for reconciliation and for expanding schools and clinics. From the late 1990s, facing a strong opposition, he leaned on war veterans and land seizures to keep power. He blamed the economic collapse on Western sanctions and saboteurs, and his government responded to inflation with price controls and arrests of shopkeepers rather than with budget cuts. The hyperinflation of 2007-08 happened under him and largely because of his government's choices.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The political decisions behind the second worst hyperinflation in history were his.
spotlights.memory_hook: He fixed prices by decree, and the shelves answered by emptying.

spotlights.name: Fast-track land reform and the tobacco collapse
spotlights.spot_it: Wide fields of broad-leaved tobacco plants, and curing barns in the Zimbabwean highveld.
spotlights.story_md: Tobacco was Zimbabwe's largest export, grown on about 1,500 large commercial farms with irrigation, credit and decades of know-how. After the seizures that began in 2000, the land went to thousands of new growers who often lacked seed, fertiliser, tractors and bank loans, since banks could no longer use farmland as collateral. The crop fell from a record of about **237 million kg in 2000** to around **49 million kg in 2008**, roughly 79 percent. Export earnings, foreign currency and tax revenue fell with it, and food production collapsed too. The industry later recovered through contract farming: output passed 250 million kg in 2018, now from tens of thousands of small growers.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The real economy shrank first; the printing press filled the gap.
spotlights.memory_hook: When the farms stopped, the presses started.

spotlights.name: Gideon Gono
spotlights.spot_it: A broad-faced banker in a dark suit, whose signature is on every note of the 2007-08 series up to the 100 trillion.
spotlights.story_md: Gideon Gono ran the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe from December 2003 to November 2013. He openly described his printing as necessary 'extraordinary' measures in a country under sanctions, and wrote a book in 2008 called *Zimbabwe's Casino Economy*. The bank funded tractors, buses and subsidies, and in 2008 sent runners into the streets with bags of Zimbabwe dollars to buy US dollars and rand on the black market. In 2009 he received the satirical **Ig Nobel Prize in Mathematics** for giving people 'a simple, everyday way to cope with a wide range of numbers' by printing notes from one cent to one hundred trillion dollars. He did not collect it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: His signature is on the most famous notes of the century.
spotlights.memory_hook: From one cent to one hundred trillion: an Ig Nobel in mathematics.

spotlights.name: Bearer cheques and agro-cheques
spotlights.spot_it: Notes headed 'Bearer Cheque' with an expiry date printed on them, as if money could go off like milk.
spotlights.story_md: From 2003 the Reserve Bank stopped issuing ordinary banknotes and issued 'bearer cheques' instead: notes with an expiry date, meant to be temporary. In practice they became the currency, in ever larger values. In January 2008 came Z$1 million, 5 million and 10 million. In May 2008 there were cheques for 100 million and 250 million; on 15 May a 500 million cheque worth about 2.50 US dollars; on 20 May 'agro-cheques' for 5, 25 and 50 billion. Each new denomination meant fresh queues at banks, which rationed cash withdrawals. Shoppers carried notes in carrier bags and paid by weight or by the brick.
spotlights.why_it_matters: An expiry date printed on money tells you everything about the state's confidence in it.
spotlights.memory_hook: Money with a use-by date.

sections.title: Zimbabwe 2008: life at 24.7 hours
sections.intro_md:
The last official inflation figure, for July 2008, was **231 million percent** a year. After that, officials stopped publishing. The economist Steve Hanke estimated the rest from black-market exchange rates and parallel prices: at the peak in **mid-November 2008**, prices rose **79.6 billion percent in a month**, about **98 percent a day**, doubling every **24.7 hours**.

Teachers and nurses stopped coming to work because a month's salary did not cover the bus fare. Harare's water utility stopped buying treatment chemicals, and a **cholera** epidemic beginning in August 2008 infected nearly 100,000 people and killed more than 4,000. ATMs and card machines failed because the numbers overflowed their software. Families survived on remittances, rural relatives, and US dollars and rand traded illegally on every corner. Banks rationed withdrawals; shoppers carried bricks of notes in plastic bags.

On 1 August 2008 the bank removed ten more zeros. On 2 February 2009 it removed twelve. In all, 25 zeros were struck off: one dollar of 2009 equalled 10 to the power 25 of the original 1980 dollars.

spotlights.name: The cholera epidemic of 2008-09
spotlights.spot_it: Queues at water points with plastic buckets, and canvas treatment tents in Harare's suburbs.
spotlights.story_md: Cholera is a disease of broken water and sewage systems, and Zimbabwe's broke because of money. The water utility could no longer pay for imported treatment chemicals, pipes burst and were not repaired, and refuse went uncollected. The outbreak began in August 2008 in Harare's Chitungwiza suburb. By late November the UN counted nearly 400 deaths; by mid-2009 there had been close to 100,000 cases and more than 4,000 deaths. Hospitals were short of staff because nurses could not afford to travel to work. It is the clearest example of how a monetary collapse kills people: not through prices directly, but by stopping everything that money keeps running.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Hyperinflation is not only an economics story; it is a public-health one.
spotlights.memory_hook: The currency died, then the water system, then people.

spotlights.name: The Trillion Dollar Campaign
spotlights.spot_it: A billboard or flyer printed directly on real Zimbabwean banknotes, with the line 'It is cheaper to print this on money than on paper.'
spotlights.story_md: The Zimbabwean was an exile newspaper printed in South Africa. In 2008 the Mugabe government slapped a 55 percent import duty on it to price it out of reach. Its ad agency, **TBWA Hunt Lascaris** in Johannesburg, answered with a campaign printed on actual Z$ notes, mostly the worthless ones, pasted into billboards, posters and flyers. Lines included 'Thanks to Mugabe, this money is wallpaper' and 'It is cheaper to print this on money than on paper.' It won the Outdoor Grand Prix at Cannes Lions and a D&AD Black Pencil, and the V&A in London now holds examples. It may be the only billboard campaign whose medium was also its message.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A design classic: the most direct possible way to show what the currency was worth.
spotlights.memory_hook: Cheaper to print the ad on money than on paper.

sections.title: Zimbabwe after: dollars, bond notes and gold
sections.intro_md:
In early 2009 a unity government with the opposition MDC legalised foreign currencies, and on **12 April 2009** the Zimbabwe dollar was suspended. Inflation vanished almost overnight: prices were now in US dollars and rand. In January 2014 the Reserve Bank even added the **Indian rupee**, the Chinese yuan, the Japanese yen and the Australian dollar to the currencies people could hold accounts and trade in, bringing the list to nine.

Dollarisation solved inflation but created a chronic shortage of physical dollars. From 2016 the bank issued **bond notes**, declared equal to US dollars; nobody believed it, and they traded at a discount. In 2019 they became the core of a revived **Zimbabwe dollar** (ZWL), which passed 30,000 per US dollar by April 2024.

In April 2024 came the sixth attempt since 2008: **Zimbabwe Gold**, or **ZiG**, announced on 5 April, trading from 8 April, partly backed by gold and foreign reserves.

spotlights.name: ZiG: Zimbabwe Gold
spotlights.spot_it: Notes with the Chiremba balancing rocks and the word ZiG, and a currency code ZWG.
spotlights.story_md: The ZiG was launched in April 2024 with the claim that it was backed by about **US$1.6 billion** of gold, foreign cash and other precious metals. It started at 13.56 per dollar. Within six months the black-market rate had nearly halved its value, and on 27 September 2024 the central bank devalued it by about 43 percent and raised interest rates to 35 percent. Since then it has been unusually stable, near 25 to 27 per dollar. In January 2026 annual ZiG inflation fell to **4.1 percent**, the first single-digit reading in almost 30 years, and to **2.9 percent** in August 2026. The central bank's stated plan is to make the ZiG the sole legal tender by 2030.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Zimbabwe's sixth try at its own money since 2008, and the first that has held for two years.
spotlights.memory_hook: Gold behind it, the dollar beside it, and the memory of 2008 in front of it.

sections.title: Venezuela: the oil state that ran out of money
sections.intro_md:
Venezuela sits on the world's largest proven oil reserves, and for decades its bolivar was one of Latin America's steadiest currencies. That ended on **18 February 1983**, 'Viernes Negro' (Black Friday), when falling oil prices forced a devaluation. Inflation stayed high for twenty years: 84 percent in 1989, 100 percent in 1996.

**Hugo Chavez**, president from 1999, spent the oil boom on social programmes and nationalisations. After a 2002-03 strike at the state oil company PDVSA, he fired thousands of its staff, and in 2003 imposed **currency controls**: dollars could be bought only from a state board, CADIVI, at an official rate. Price controls followed.

Chavez died in March 2013. Under his successor **Nicolas Maduro**, oil prices crashed from mid-2014, and oil earned almost all of Venezuela's foreign currency. The government kept spending and the central bank (BCV) financed it. Inflation was 69 percent in 2014, 181 percent in 2015, and in **November 2016** monthly inflation passed 50 percent. Venezuela became the 57th hyperinflation on record.

spotlights.name: Hugo Chavez
spotlights.spot_it: A broad-faced former paratrooper in a red shirt or red beret, often holding a small blue copy of the constitution.
spotlights.story_md: Hugo Chavez, a former army officer who had led a failed coup in 1992, won the 1998 election promising to share Venezuela's oil wealth with the poor. With oil prices soaring through the 2000s, he funded housing, clinics, food subsidies and cheap petrol, and poverty fell. He also nationalised firms, imposed currency and price controls from 2003, and turned PDVSA into a tool for social spending, starving it of investment. Oil production, about 3 million barrels a day around 1998, began a long slide. When he died in 2013, he left a state that spent as if oil would always be expensive.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The policies that made hyperinflation possible were built in the boom years.
spotlights.memory_hook: He spent a boom as if it were permanent.

spotlights.name: Nicolas Maduro
spotlights.spot_it: A tall man with a thick black moustache, often in a tracksuit top in the colours of the Venezuelan flag.
spotlights.story_md: A former Caracas bus driver and union leader, Nicolas Maduro was Chavez's foreign minister and chosen heir. He took office in April 2013 with inflation at 29 percent. As oil prices fell he blamed an 'economic war' by businesses and foreign enemies, sent troops into electronics shops to force price cuts, and kept financing the state through the central bank. The BCV stopped publishing data from 2015 to 2019. US financial sanctions from 2017 and oil sanctions from 2019 deepened the collapse. From 2019 his government quietly relaxed controls and tolerated dollars. On **3 January 2026** he was seized in a US military operation and taken to the United States.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He presided over the deepest economic collapse in modern Latin American history.
spotlights.memory_hook: He blamed an economic war; the printing press was his own.

spotlights.name: PDVSA and the oil collapse
spotlights.spot_it: The red PDVSA logo on offices, petrol pumps and tanker trucks all over Venezuela.
spotlights.story_md: Oil earned the overwhelming majority of Venezuela's export income, so the price of a barrel was, in effect, the price of the bolivar. The state oil company PDVSA lost thousands of skilled staff after 2003, was loaded with social programmes and borrowing, and its fields and refineries decayed. Output, around 3 million barrels a day in the late 1990s, fell to about 2.4 million in 2015, 1.34 million by the end of 2018 and, after US oil sanctions in 2019 and the pandemic, to a level PDVSA itself put at about 374,000 barrels a day in mid-2020, the lowest since 1945. Fewer barrels at lower prices meant fewer dollars, and the gap was filled with bolivars.
spotlights.why_it_matters: An oil state's currency is only as strong as its oil company.
spotlights.memory_hook: When the oil stopped flowing, the bolivars started.

sections.title: Venezuela 2016 to 2021: the everyday collapse
sections.intro_md:
Venezuela's hyperinflation ran from November 2016 to about the end of 2021, more than four years: much longer than Weimar's or Zimbabwe's peak. The official central bank number for 2018 was **130,060 percent**; the opposition-run National Assembly put it at about 1.7 million percent; the IMF at about 930,000 percent. From 2016 to April 2019, by the BCV's own count, prices rose about **53.8 million percent**.

The minimum wage was about 360 US dollars a month in 2012. By April 2019 it was worth about **5.50 dollars**, less than a McDonald's Happy Meal. In a 2017 university survey (ENCOVI), Venezuelans reported losing on average about **11 kg** of body weight in a year. Shops at Christmas 2017 gave up on price tags. Young people farmed gold in the online game *RuneScape* and sold it for dollars. And people left: by late 2024 about **7.9 million** Venezuelans had emigrated, many of them on foot.

spotlights.name: Handbags woven from bolivars
spotlights.spot_it: Purses, wallets and birds folded from hundreds of small banknotes, sold on the streets of Cucuta.
spotlights.story_md: In 2018 Venezuelan migrants in the Colombian border city of Cucuta found that their notes were worth more as material than as money. Artisans folded small bills into strips and wove them into handbags, wallets, belts, crowns and bird sculptures. One seller, Alvaro Rivera, made his largest handbag from 1,000 notes with a face value of 100,000 bolivars: about 17 US cents at the exchange houses. The bag sold for about 13 dollars. Another, Jesus Campos, told the Christian Science Monitor that the notes in one of his bags would not buy a coffee back home.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A currency's real value made visible: as fibre, it was worth 75 times more.
spotlights.memory_hook: A purse made of money is worth more than the money.

spotlights.name: The exodus across the Simon Bolivar bridge
spotlights.spot_it: Crowds walking across a concrete bridge over a narrow river, carrying suitcases and children.
spotlights.story_md: The Simon Bolivar International Bridge joins San Antonio del Tachira in Venezuela to Cucuta in Colombia. At the height of the crisis tens of thousands of people crossed it on some days: to buy food and medicine in Colombia and walk back, or to leave for good. Many walked on to Bogota, Quito, Lima and Santiago, a journey of weeks. By November 2024 about **7.9 million** Venezuelans lived abroad, with more than 6.7 million in Latin America and the Caribbean. Their remittances became one of the main sources of dollars for the families left behind, helping to dollarise the economy from below.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Hyperinflation's largest human consequence was migration on a scale few countries outside war have seen.
spotlights.memory_hook: A whole country walked across one bridge.

spotlights.name: 'Thank God it exists': dollars take over
spotlights.spot_it: A street market where every price is chalked in dollars and change is given in bolivars.
spotlights.story_md: By 2019 Venezuelans had largely abandoned the bolivar for anything larger than a bus fare, paying in dollar notes, remittances, Zelle transfers from US accounts, or Colombian pesos near the border. In a television interview broadcast on 17 November 2019, Maduro, whose government had spent years jailing currency traders, called this dollarisation an 'escape valve' and said: 'gracias a Dios existe', thank God it exists. The government relaxed price controls and stopped prosecuting dollar deals. Inflation slowed. The bolivar remained the legal currency, but in practice Venezuela joined Zimbabwe 2009: the street had chosen its money before the state did.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Spontaneous dollarisation, not a reform plan, broke the hyperinflation.
spotlights.memory_hook: The president who blamed the dollar ended up thanking God for it.

spotlights.name: Fourteen zeros in thirteen years
spotlights.spot_it: Bolivar fuerte notes of 2017 in values up to 100,000, each carrying a national hero, all wiped out by later cuts of zeros.
spotlights.story_md: Venezuela redenominated three times. In 2008 the **bolivar fuerte** dropped three zeros. In August 2018 the **bolivar soberano** dropped five more, as the minimum wage was raised from about 393,000 old bolivars to 180 million (1,800 new ones). On 1 October 2021 the **bolivar digital** dropped six more: everything was divided by a million, and the official dollar rate went overnight from 4.18 million to 4.18. In total, 14 zeros vanished in 13 years: one bolivar digital equals 100 trillion of the bolivars of 2007. In 2018 the government also launched the **Petro**, an oil-backed state cryptocurrency; it never caught on and was shut down on 15 January 2024.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Cutting zeros changes the labels, not the disease.
spotlights.memory_hook: Fourteen zeros gone, and the price of a coffee still climbing.

sections.title: Three collapses side by side
sections.intro_md:
**Weimar** was the shortest and sharpest: roughly 16 months of true hyperinflation in 1922-23, triggered by war debt, reparations and the Ruhr strike, and ended within weeks by a new currency and a balanced budget. **Zimbabwe** was a slow-motion disaster that turned vertical: a decade of decline after the land seizures, then an explosion in 2007-08 that peaked faster than Germany's, ended not by reform but by abandoning the national currency. **Venezuela** was the longest: more than four years above Cagan's line, with lower monthly peaks but enormous human costs, ended by the population switching to dollars.

The common thread is political: a budget hole nobody would close, a central bank that was not independent, statistics that vanished, controls that emptied shops. Each cure restored one thing: belief that the money supply had a limit.
