sections.title: How hyperinflations end
sections.intro_md:
Hyperinflations always end. The question is how much damage is done first. History offers three exits.

**1. A credible new currency with a hard limit.** Germany 1923, Austria 1922, Hungary 1946, Yugoslavia 1994. The new money works only if the central bank stops lending to the government and the budget is brought close to balance. Thomas Sargent showed in 1982 that in the interwar cases prices stopped rising almost at once, without the long recession many economists expected, because people believed the change of regime was real.

**2. Use someone else's money.** Zimbabwe 2009, and Ecuador, which adopted the US dollar in 2000 after a currency collapse. The government gives up printing altogether. Prices stabilise at once, but the country loses its own monetary policy.

**3. Let the street decide.** Venezuela after 2019: the state never formally reformed, but people moved to dollars and the government stopped fighting it. It works, slowly and unequally.

What does not work: price controls, arrests of shopkeepers, cutting zeros, or a new name on the same old printing press.

spotlights.name: Thomas Sargent and 'The Ends of Four Big Inflations'
spotlights.spot_it: A white-haired economist with glasses, Nobel laureate of 2011.
spotlights.story_md: In 1982 the American economist Thomas Sargent studied how the hyperinflations of Austria, Hungary, Poland and Germany ended in 1922-24. His finding upset the conventional wisdom that stopping inflation requires years of painful unemployment. In each case, prices stopped rising almost immediately once two things happened together: the government credibly changed its budget regime, and the central bank was made independent and barred from financing deficits. The change worked because people believed it. Critics argue he underplays reparations and foreign loans, but the paper became a foundation of modern central banking. Sargent shared the 2011 Nobel Prize in economics.
spotlights.why_it_matters: His paper is why central banks today are made independent of finance ministries.
spotlights.memory_hook: Change the regime, not just the money, and inflation stops overnight.

sections.title: India: close calls, never the cliff
sections.intro_md:
India has never had a hyperinflation, but it has seen what high inflation does, and its institutions were shaped by those episodes.

During the **Second World War** the colonial government paid for huge military spending in India largely by printing rupees, while Britain settled its bills with IOUs held in London, the 'sterling balances'. Food prices soared, and wartime inflation is one cause historians and Amartya Sen identify for the **Bengal famine of 1943**, in which, by most estimates, 2 to 3 million people died. In **1973-74**, after the oil shock and drought, wholesale inflation hit about **25 percent** for the year. In **1991** India came within weeks of default and flew **47 tonnes of gold** to the Bank of England as collateral; the crisis launched liberalisation.

Since 2016 the RBI has had a legal target: **4 percent** consumer inflation, band 2 to 6 percent, renewed in March 2026 for 2026 to 2031. And in a twist, the **rupee** was one of nine currencies Zimbabwe allowed in 2014, while it had no money of its own.

spotlights.name: Wartime printing and the Bengal famine
spotlights.spot_it: Photographs of emaciated families on Calcutta pavements in 1943.
spotlights.story_md: When Japan took Burma in 1942, Bengal became a front line. The British Indian government built airfields and camps on a vast scale and paid largely with new notes. Banglapedia notes that printing notes financed war expenditure to a great extent; rice imports from Burma stopped, a cyclone hit in October 1942, and boats and stocks were seized under a 'denial' policy. Prices of rice rose several times over. Amartya Sen's study argued that people died not simply because there was no food, but because labourers' wages could no longer buy it. Inflation was one engine of that: money flowed to those working for the war economy, while rural labourers were priced out.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Inflation does not need to be hyper to kill; it needs to outrun the wages of the poor.
spotlights.memory_hook: In 1943 rice did not vanish; it was priced out of reach.

spotlights.name: The 1991 gold airlift
spotlights.spot_it: Crates of gold bars loaded secretly onto a chartered plane at Mumbai.
spotlights.story_md: By January 1991 India's foreign exchange reserves had fallen to about **1.2 billion dollars**, and by June they covered barely three weeks of imports. To borrow, the government used gold: in May 1991 about 20 tonnes went to UBS in Switzerland, and in July the Reserve Bank flew about **47 tonnes** to the Bank of England, pledged to it and the Bank of Japan. When the news came out, it caused a public outcry. In July the rupee was devalued by about 18 percent in two steps, and Finance Minister Manmohan Singh's budget opened the economy. India did not suffer a currency collapse because it acted before one. In 2024 the RBI brought 100 tonnes of its gold home from the UK.
spotlights.why_it_matters: India's closest brush with a currency crisis, and the start of its modern economy.
spotlights.memory_hook: Gold flew out to save the rupee, and came home 33 years later.

spotlights.name: The RBI's 4 percent target
spotlights.spot_it: A monetary policy committee statement that begins with the CPI figure and the 4 percent goal.
spotlights.story_md: India adopted formal inflation targeting in 2015-16: the government and the RBI agreed on a goal of **4 percent** consumer price inflation, with a tolerance band of 2 to 6 percent, written into the RBI Act. A six-member Monetary Policy Committee sets the repo rate to hit it. The framework was renewed in 2021 and, by a notification of March 2026, for April 2026 to March 2031. It is the opposite philosophy to the hyperinflating central banks of today's story: a central bank with one clear number, independent of the finance ministry's short-term needs. Inflation fell to a record low of 0.25 percent in October 2025, below the band.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is India's institutional insurance against the slide that began in Weimar, Harare and Caracas.
spotlights.memory_hook: Four percent, plus or minus two: a promise written into law.

spotlights.name: The rupee in Zimbabwe
spotlights.spot_it: Indian rupee notes with Gandhi's portrait, listed on a Harare bank's currency board.
spotlights.story_md: Five years after abandoning its own dollar, Zimbabwe still had too few physical US dollars. In January 2014 the Reserve Bank announced that, besides the US dollar, rand, pula, pound and euro, people and companies could also open accounts and trade in the **Indian rupee**, the Chinese yuan, the Japanese yen and the Australian dollar, making nine foreign currencies in all. The bank cited growing trade and investment with India and China. In practice few rupee notes ever circulated in Harare, but for a while a country that had printed 100 trillion dollar notes listed India's currency as one of its own.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A small, true link between India and one of the worst hyperinflations ever.
spotlights.memory_hook: For a while, Gandhi's face was legal in Harare.

sections.title: Myths and half-truths
sections.intro_md:
Hyperinflation attracts stories that are too good to check. Some are true, some half true, some invented.

**'Hyperinflation brought Hitler to power.'** Half true at best: see the spotlight below. Research by Galofre-Vila and colleagues finds Nazi votes rose most where Chancellor Bruning's austerity cuts of 1930-32 were deepest. The inflation's real legacy was a ruined, bitter middle class and a German fear of inflation that lasts to this day.

**'A man left a wheelbarrow of money outside a shop, and thieves stole the barrow and left the money.'** A good joke, told about Weimar and many other places. No one has documented it.

**'Printing money always causes hyperinflation.'** No. Many central banks created vast sums after 2008 and in 2020 without it. Hyperinflation comes when a government cannot pay its way, the central bank must fund it, and people know it.

**'Gold backing prevents it.'** Not necessarily: Zimbabwe's gold-backed ZiG lost about half its value in its first six months.

spotlights.name: Munich, November 1923: the putsch that failed
spotlights.spot_it: Armed men with swastika armbands at a barricade in Munich, November 1923.
spotlights.story_md: On 8 November 1923, with the mark at billions to the dollar, Adolf Hitler and his followers tried to seize power in Munich, hoping to march on Berlin. Police opened fire the next day at the Odeonsplatz; the coup collapsed and Hitler went to prison, where he wrote *Mein Kampf*. A week later the Rentenmark arrived and the currency stabilised. In the calmer years that followed, the Nazis were a fringe party: 2.6 percent of the vote in May 1928. They became the largest party in July 1932, amid deflation, cuts and six million unemployed. The hyperinflation weakened faith in the republic, but it was the Depression that delivered the votes.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It corrects the most common lesson people draw from Weimar.
spotlights.memory_hook: Hyperinflation gave Hitler a failed putsch; the Depression gave him votes.

spotlights.name: Keynes, Lenin and 'debauching the currency'
spotlights.spot_it: A tall Englishman with a moustache, in a three-piece suit, who wrote the most famous warning about inflation.
spotlights.story_md: In *The Economic Consequences of the Peace* (1919), John Maynard Keynes wrote: 'Lenin is said to have declared that the best way to destroy the Capitalist System was to debauch the currency.' He added that there is 'no subtler, no surer means of overturning the existing basis of society'. The line is quoted constantly, usually as Lenin's. But nobody has found the remark in Lenin's own writings; Keynes himself wrote only that Lenin 'is said to have' said it. The book itself was prophetic, arguing that harsh reparations would ruin Germany's finances. Four years later the German currency was destroyed.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A great quotation, rightly Keynes's, doubtfully Lenin's.
spotlights.memory_hook: Keynes said Lenin said it; Lenin never said it anywhere we can find.

sections.title: Now: 2025 to 2026
sections.intro_md:
Hyperinflation is not history. As of October 2026:

**Venezuela** (as of September 2026). Inflation was **475 percent** in 2025, the world's highest. On **3 January 2026** US forces captured Nicolas Maduro; **Delcy Rodriguez** became acting president. Monthly inflation peaked at **32.6 percent in January 2026**, just below Cagan's line, then slowed. The official rate went from about 301 bolivars per dollar in January to **827.73** on 10 September.

**Zimbabwe** (as of September 2026). Annual ZiG inflation fell to **4.1 percent** in January 2026, the first single-digit reading in almost 30 years, and **2.9 percent** in August; the central bank says it will make the ZiG the only legal tender by 2030.

**Iran** (as of July 2026). War and sanctions pushed the rial to a record **1,918,000 per dollar** on 17 July 2026; the IMF expects inflation near 69 percent this year: very high, not yet hyper.

**Argentina** (January 2026). After 211 percent in 2023 and 118 percent in 2024, inflation fell to **31.5 percent** in 2025, the lowest since 2017.

spotlights.name: Venezuela after Maduro
spotlights.spot_it: A Caracas market where every stall chalks prices in bolivars and every buyer works them out in dollars.
spotlights.story_md: NPR reported from the Quinta Crespo market in Caracas three weeks after Maduro's capture: fish priced in bolivars, everyone calculating in dollars, and a pensioner whose monthly pension of 130 bolivars was worth under 40 cents. The first sales of Venezuelan oil by the United States brought a trickle of dollars that steadied prices for a while. The central bank, silent for over a year, published figures again in March 2026: 475 percent for 2025, food prices up 532 percent. Monthly inflation peaked at 32.6 percent in January and fell to 6.3 percent by May, though the bolivar kept sliding, past 800 to the dollar by September. Workers and pensioners protest for wages.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The world's highest inflation now sits inside a country in political transition.
spotlights.memory_hook: New government, old currency, and prices still worked out in dollars.

spotlights.name: Zimbabwe's single-digit year
spotlights.spot_it: A Zimstat release with a single-digit figure on its first line.
spotlights.story_md: On 27 January 2026 Zimbabwe announced annual ZiG inflation of **4.1 percent**, and US-dollar inflation of 1 percent: the first single-digit reading for its own currency in almost 30 years. The figure kept falling, to 3.2 percent in July and 2.9 percent in August, the lowest since 1980 according to the Reserve Bank, before edging up to about 3.7 percent in September. Most transactions are still in US dollars, reserves cover only about a month of imports, and businesses fear the plan to make the ZiG the sole legal tender by 2030. But for the country that gave the world the 100 trillion dollar note, two years of a stable currency is news.
spotlights.why_it_matters: If it holds, Zimbabwe will have done what Germany did in 1923, just much more slowly.
spotlights.memory_hook: From 100 trillion to 4 percent in seventeen years.

spotlights.name: Argentina's long fever breaks, for now
spotlights.spot_it: A man with long sideburns and unruly hair, famous for waving a chainsaw at rallies.
spotlights.story_md: Argentina has had more inflation crises than almost any country, including a hyperinflation in 1989-90. By 2023 inflation had reached 211 percent a year and the economist **Javier Milei** won the presidency waving a chainsaw at state spending. His government devalued the peso, slashed spending, stopped central-bank financing of the Treasury and ran a fiscal surplus. Inflation fell to 117.8 percent in 2024 and **31.5 percent** in 2025, the lowest since 2017, with December 2025 at 2.8 percent a month. Critics point to the social cost, a strong peso and frozen wages. Supporters say it is Sargent's lesson again: change the fiscal regime and prices follow.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A live test of the oldest cure for high inflation: stop financing deficits with new money.
spotlights.memory_hook: A chainsaw for the budget, a brake for prices.

sections.title: Recap
sections.intro_md:
1. **Hyperinflation** means prices rising more than **50 percent a month** (Cagan, 1956). There have been about 57 episodes; the worst was Hungary in 1946, with prices doubling every 15 hours.
2. The recipe: a budget hole, a central bank that fills it, then a flip in expectations.
3. **Weimar 1923**: war debt, reparations, the Ruhr strike; 4.2 trillion marks to the dollar; ended in weeks by the **Rentenmark** and a hard limit on money.
4. **Zimbabwe 2008**: land seizures wrecked exports, the Reserve Bank printed; prices doubled every **24.7 hours**; the **100 trillion** note; ended by dropping the currency. Its gold-backed **ZiG** reached single-digit inflation in 2026.
5. **Venezuela 2016-21**: oil crash, controls, a printing central bank; 130,060 percent in 2018; 14 zeros cut; 7.9 million emigrants; ended by street dollarisation. Still 475 percent in 2025.
6. Recognise: banknote wallpaper, Notgeld, Bayer's Bauhaus note, bearer cheques, the Trillion Dollar Campaign, bolivar handbags.
7. India never crossed the line, and since 2016 its central bank has a legal 4 percent target.

cards.front: What is Cagan's definition of hyperinflation?
cards.back: Prices rising more than 50 percent in a single month (about 13,000 percent a year if sustained).

cards.front: Which country holds the world record for hyperinflation, and when?
cards.back: Hungary, peaking in July 1946, with prices doubling about every 15 hours.

cards.front: How many marks did one US dollar buy in November 1923?
cards.back: About 4.2 trillion (4,210,500,000,000), compared with 4.2 marks in 1914.

cards.front: Why did the occupation of the Ruhr turn German inflation into hyperinflation?
cards.back: The government ordered passive resistance and paid millions of striking workers with newly printed money, while losing the Ruhr's output and taxes.

cards.front: What is happening in this 1923 photo, and why?
cards.back: Banknotes used as wallpaper: by late 1923 the paper was worth more than the money.

cards.front: What replaced the paper mark in November 1923, and at what rate?
cards.back: The Rentenmark, on 15 November 1923: one Rentenmark for one trillion paper marks.

cards.front: Why did the Rentenmark work though it had no gold behind it?
cards.back: Its quantity was strictly capped and the central bank stopped lending to the government, so people believed it would hold its value.

cards.front: Name this banknote and the year it was issued.
cards.back: Zimbabwe's 100 trillion dollar note, issued 16 January 2009.

cards.front: What was Zimbabwe's peak monthly inflation and doubling time?
cards.back: About 79.6 billion percent in mid-November 2008; prices doubled every 24.7 hours (Hanke estimate).

cards.front: What set off Zimbabwe's economic collapse after 2000?
cards.back: Fast-track land reform seized commercial farms; farm output and exports such as tobacco collapsed, so the state printed money to fill the gap.

cards.front: How did Zimbabwe's hyperinflation end in 2009?
cards.back: The government legalised foreign currencies and suspended the Zimbabwe dollar on 12 April 2009; the US dollar and rand took over.

cards.front: What is the ZiG?
cards.back: Zimbabwe Gold, the currency launched in April 2024, partly backed by gold and reserves; Zimbabwe's sixth attempt at its own money since 2008.

cards.front: When did Venezuela enter hyperinflation, and what was the official 2018 rate?
cards.back: November 2016; the central bank reported 130,060 percent for 2018.

cards.front: Why did Venezuela's oil collapse matter so much for the bolivar?
cards.back: Oil earned almost all its foreign currency; when prices and output fell, the government kept spending and the central bank printed the difference.

cards.front: How many zeros did Venezuela remove from its currency between 2008 and 2021?
cards.back: Fourteen: 3 in 2008, 5 in 2018 and 6 in 2021.

cards.front: How did Venezuela's hyperinflation actually end?
cards.back: Mostly through spontaneous dollarisation from 2019, which the government tolerated and relaxed controls around.

cards.front: What did Thomas Sargent conclude in 'The Ends of Four Big Inflations'?
cards.back: Interwar hyperinflations stopped almost at once when governments credibly changed their fiscal regime and barred the central bank from financing deficits.

cards.front: What is the RBI's inflation target?
cards.back: 4 percent consumer price inflation, with a band of 2 to 6 percent; renewed for April 2026 to March 2031.

cards.front: What happened to India's gold in 1991?
cards.back: About 20 tonnes went to UBS in May and about 47 tonnes to the Bank of England in July, as collateral for loans during the balance-of-payments crisis.

cards.front: What was Venezuela's inflation in 2025, and what happened in January 2026?
cards.back: 475 percent, the world's highest; on 3 January 2026 US forces captured Nicolas Maduro.

cards.front: What kind of money is this, and who issued it?
cards.back: Notgeld, emergency money printed by German towns and companies when the Reichsbank could not keep up.

cards.front: Who designed emergency notes like this for Thuringia in 1923?
cards.back: Herbert Bayer of the Bauhaus.

cards.front: Who is this, and what did he run?
cards.back: Rudolf Havenstein, president of the Reichsbank 1908 to 1923.

cards.front: Who is this banker, and what did he do in November 1923?
cards.back: Hjalmar Schacht, currency commissioner, who stopped the Reichsbank lending to the government.

cards.front: What does this stamped note show?
cards.back: A 1,000-mark note overprinted in 1923 as one billion marks.

cards.front: What is this note, and what was it worth?
cards.back: A Rentenmark note dated 1 November 1923; one Rentenmark equalled one trillion paper marks.

cards.front: This Hungarian note of 1946 was printed but never issued. What was its value?
cards.back: One milliard b-pengo: one sextillion (10 to the 21st) pengo, ten times the largest note actually issued.

cards.front: Who is this, and which central bank did he run?
cards.back: Gideon Gono, Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe, 2003 to 2013.

cards.front: What are these, and what was odd about them?
cards.back: Zimbabwean bearer cheques: banknotes with a printed expiry date.

cards.front: Which leader is this, and how did his rule end?
cards.back: Robert Mugabe, removed by a military takeover in November 2017.

cards.front: Who is this, and when did he rule Venezuela?
cards.back: Hugo Chavez, president 1999 to 2013.

cards.front: Who is this, and what happened to him on 3 January 2026?
cards.back: Nicolas Maduro, captured by US forces.

cards.front: What were Venezuelan migrants making from these in 2018?
cards.back: Bolivar notes woven into handbags, wallets and crafts, worth more than the money itself.

cards.front: Which is the hyperinflation-era paper mark and which is the Rentenmark?
cards.back: Left: a 1923 overprinted paper mark. Right: the Rentenmark that ended the inflation.

cards.front: What is the Olivera-Tanzi effect?
cards.back: In high inflation, taxes lose value between assessment and payment, so real revenue collapses and the deficit grows.

cards.front: Gresham's law says bad money drives out good; in hyperinflation the reverse, called ____ law, applies.
cards.back: Thiers' law: people switch to stable money such as dollars.

cards.front: Who was Hugo Stinnes?
cards.back: A German industrialist who borrowed paper marks to buy real assets during the inflation, the classic winner of 1923.

cards.front: What was the Trillion Dollar Campaign?
cards.back: A 2009 campaign for The Zimbabwean newspaper printed on real Zimbabwean banknotes, by TBWA Hunt Lascaris.

cards.front: What was CADIVI?
cards.back: Venezuela's currency-control board, created in February 2003, the only legal seller of dollars at an official rate.

cards.front: How many Venezuelans had emigrated by late 2024?
cards.back: About 7.9 million.

cards.front: In 2017 Venezuelans reported losing about ____ kg of body weight on average (ENCOVI survey).
cards.back: 11 kg.

cards.front: Did hyperinflation bring Hitler to power?
cards.back: Not directly: his 1923 putsch failed, the Nazis had 2.6 percent in 1928, and their surge came in the 1930-33 Depression and austerity.

cards.front: Who actually wrote the line about Lenin and 'debauching the currency'?
cards.back: Keynes, in 1919, saying Lenin 'is said to have' declared it; no Lenin source is known.

cards.front: What link did Zimbabwe have with the Indian rupee?
cards.back: In January 2014 the rupee was one of four Asian and Pacific currencies added to Zimbabwe's multi-currency system.

cards.front: How did wartime inflation contribute to the Bengal famine of 1943?
cards.back: War spending financed largely by printing notes pushed rice prices beyond what rural labourers' wages could buy.

cards.front: What was Zimbabwe's annual ZiG inflation in January 2026?
cards.back: 4.1 percent, the first single-digit reading in almost 30 years.

cards.front: What was Argentina's inflation in 2025?
cards.back: 31.5 percent, the lowest since 2017, after 211 percent in 2023.

cards.front: What was the 'adopengo'?
cards.back: Hungary's 1946 tax pengo, a unit whose value was announced daily by radio to protect tax revenue.

cards.front: How did Yugoslavia end its 1993-94 hyperinflation?
cards.back: A new dinar pegged one-to-one to the Deutsche Mark in January 1994, under governor Dragoslav Avramovic.

cards.front: What is money illusion?
cards.back: The tendency to think in nominal amounts (the number on the note) rather than in real purchasing power.

cards.front: Who coined the term 'money illusion' and in which book?
cards.back: Irving Fisher, in The Money Illusion (1928).

cards.front: What is this, and which country made it?
cards.back: A Z$100 trillion banknote; Zimbabwe's notes later became collectors' items worth far more than their face value.

quiz.prompt: Why did Germany's inflation turn into hyperinflation in 1923?
quiz.explanation: The Ruhr occupation and passive resistance, financed by printing money, on top of war debt and reparations.
options: A stock market crash in New York
Paying Ruhr strikers with printed money

quiz.prompt: What is this?
quiz.explanation: A Zimbabwean 100 trillion dollar note of 2009.

quiz.prompt: Which picture shows the currency that ended Germany's hyperinflation?
quiz.explanation: Right: the Rentenmark of November 1923. Left: an overprinted paper mark.

quiz.prompt: Put these hyperinflations in order, earliest first.
quiz.explanation: France 1795-96, Germany 1923, Hungary 1946, Yugoslavia 1993-94, Zimbabwe 2008, Venezuela 2016-21.

quiz.prompt: Match each person to their role.
answer: The Ends of Four Big Inflations
quiz.explanation: Havenstein printed, Schacht stopped it, Gono printed in Harare, Cagan defined, Sargent explained the endings.
pairs: The Ends of Four Big Inflations

quiz.prompt: Tap the city where migrants wove handbags from bolivar notes in 2018.
quiz.explanation: Cucuta, the Colombian border city at the Simon Bolivar bridge.

quiz.prompt: Tap the region whose occupation in January 1923 tipped Germany into hyperinflation.
quiz.explanation: The Ruhr, around Essen and Dortmund in western Germany.

quiz.prompt: Doubling time at the peak: was Zimbabwe 2008 faster or slower than Weimar 1923?
quiz.explanation: Zimbabwe 24.7 hours; Germany about 3.7 days.

quiz.prompt: The Rentenmark was backed by gold reserves held at the Reichsbank.
quiz.explanation: It was nominally secured on a mortgage on land and industry; there was no gold behind it.

quiz.prompt: Guess the object from the clues.
quiz.explanation: Bearer cheques were Zimbabwe's 'temporary' banknotes from 2003 to 2008.
clues: It was meant to be temporary.
It had an expiry date printed on it.
Versions existed for 500 million and 50 billion.
Later issues were signed by Gideon Gono.

quiz.prompt: Which of these did NOT help end a hyperinflation?
quiz.explanation: Price controls make shortages worse; the other three ended real hyperinflations.
options: A new currency with a hard cap (Germany 1923)
A peg to the Deutsche Mark (Yugoslavia 1994)

quiz.prompt: What did the Bauhaus designer Herbert Bayer make in 1923?
quiz.explanation: Emergency banknotes for the State Bank of Thuringia, with sans-serif type and flat colour.

quiz.prompt: Venezuela's government published inflation data throughout its hyperinflation.
quiz.explanation: The central bank stopped publishing from 2015 to May 2019, and again for over a year before March 2026.

quiz.prompt: What did Maduro call Venezuela's de facto dollarisation in November 2019?
quiz.explanation: An 'escape valve', adding 'thank God it exists'.
options: An escape valve, thank God it exists

quiz.prompt: Match the currency to the country.
quiz.explanation: Each is a currency from today's story.

quiz.prompt: Which currency did Zimbabwe add to its basket in January 2014, along with the yuan, yen and Australian dollar?
quiz.explanation: The Indian rupee.

quiz.prompt: Annual inflation in 2025: Venezuela compared with Argentina?
quiz.explanation: Venezuela 475 percent; Argentina 31.5 percent.

quiz.prompt: Who is this?
quiz.explanation: Hjalmar Schacht, who as currency commissioner in November 1923 stopped the Reichsbank from financing the government.

quiz.prompt: Guess the event from the clues.
quiz.explanation: TBWA Hunt Lascaris's 2009 campaign for The Zimbabwean, printed on real banknotes.
clues: It was for an exiled newspaper.
It won a Grand Prix at Cannes.
Its billboards were made of real money.

quiz.prompt: India has never experienced a hyperinflation.
quiz.explanation: Its worst years were about 38 percent in 1943-44 and about 25 percent in 1974-75, far below 50 percent a month.

quiz_bank.prompt: A loaf of bread in Berlin cost about 160 marks at the end of 1922. About how much did it cost by late 1923?
quiz_bank.explanation: About 200 billion marks.

quiz_bank.prompt: In August 2018, how many bolivars did a 2.4 kg chicken cost in a Caracas mini-market?
quiz_bank.explanation: 14.6 million bolivars, about 2.22 US dollars, in the Reuters photo by Carlos Garcia Rawlins.

quiz_bank.prompt: Under Cagan's definition, an episode of hyperinflation ends as soon as monthly inflation drops below 50 percent.
quiz_bank.explanation: It must fall below 50 percent and stay there for at least a year.

quiz_bank.prompt: According to Peter Bernholz, what caused at least 25 of 29 hyperinflations he studied?
quiz_bank.explanation: Government budget deficits financed by creating money.
options: Budget deficits financed by money creation

quiz_bank.prompt: How did the German government respond to the French and Belgian occupation of the Ruhr in 1923?
quiz_bank.explanation: Passive resistance, with striking workers paid in newly printed money.
options: Passive resistance, paying strikers with printed money

quiz_bank.prompt: In 1923, people who owed money in paper marks generally gained from the hyperinflation.
quiz_bank.explanation: Debts shrank to nothing: 'a mark is a mark'. Hugo Stinnes and the state itself were the great winners.

quiz_bank.prompt: What backed the Rentenmark on paper?
quiz_bank.explanation: A notional mortgage on German agricultural and industrial land; its real strength was a strict cap on its quantity.
options: A mortgage on land and industry

quiz_bank.prompt: Which of these was NOT faster at its peak than Germany in 1923?
quiz_bank.explanation: Venezuela's peak months doubled prices in weeks; Hungary, Zimbabwe and Yugoslavia all beat Germany's 3.7 days.

quiz_bank.prompt: Zimbabwe's tobacco crop in 2008 compared with 2000: higher or lower?
quiz_bank.explanation: About 49 million kg in 2008 against about 237 million kg in 2000, a fall of roughly 79 percent.

quiz_bank.prompt: Why did Harare's 2008 cholera epidemic happen?
quiz_bank.explanation: The water utility could not pay for treatment chemicals and repairs as the currency collapsed.
options: The water utility stopped buying treatment chemicals

quiz_bank.prompt: Zimbabwe's gold-backed ZiG has never been devalued.
quiz_bank.explanation: It was devalued by about 43 percent in late September 2024, six months after launch.

quiz_bank.prompt: What was CADIVI in Venezuela?
quiz_bank.explanation: The currency-control board set up in 2003, the only legal seller of dollars at the official rate.

quiz_bank.prompt: Venezuela's monthly minimum wage in US dollars: April 2019 compared with 2012?
quiz_bank.explanation: About 5.50 dollars in April 2019 against about 360 dollars in 2012.

quiz_bank.prompt: Put Venezuela's currency reforms in order, earliest first.
quiz_bank.explanation: 2008 fuerte; February 2018 Petro; August 2018 soberano; October 2021 digital. Petro and soberano were both 2018: the Petro came first.

quiz_bank.prompt: Which of the three hyperinflations lasted longest above Cagan's line?
quiz_bank.explanation: Venezuela: about four years, from November 2016 to around the end of 2021.

quiz_bank.prompt: Thomas Sargent found that the interwar hyperinflations could only be stopped by years of deep recession.
quiz_bank.explanation: He found the opposite: prices stopped almost at once when a credible fiscal and central-bank regime change took place.

quiz_bank.prompt: In July 1991 India flew about 47 tonnes of gold to which institution?
quiz_bank.explanation: The Bank of England, pledged with it and the Bank of Japan; 20 tonnes had gone to UBS in May.

quiz_bank.prompt: What is the RBI's legal inflation target?
quiz_bank.explanation: 4 percent CPI inflation, band 2 to 6 percent, renewed for 2026 to 2031.

quiz_bank.prompt: What share of the vote did the Nazis win in the 1928 Reichstag election?
quiz_bank.explanation: 2.6 percent, after stabilisation. Their surge came in 1930-33.

quiz_bank.prompt: What inflation did Venezuela's central bank report for 2025?
quiz_bank.explanation: 475 percent, the highest in the world.

best_facts.fact: In Hungary in July 1946 prices doubled roughly every 15 hours, the fastest inflation ever recorded. When the forint replaced the pengo, all the Hungarian banknotes in circulation together were worth about a thousandth of a US cent.
best_facts.why_surprising: A whole nation's cash was worth less than a single coin.

best_facts.fact: Germany's entire domestic war debt of about 164 billion marks was worth just 16.4 pfennig at the currency reform of November 1923.
best_facts.why_surprising: A state wiped out a world war's worth of debt by destroying its own money.

best_facts.fact: Zimbabwe's central bank governor Gideon Gono received the 2009 Ig Nobel Prize in Mathematics for printing notes from one cent to one hundred trillion dollars.
best_facts.why_surprising: A central banker won a prize for teaching his people very large numbers.

best_facts.fact: In autumn 1923 up to 133 printing firms with 1,783 presses, 30 paper mills and about 30,000 people worked day and night to print German money, and there was still a cash shortage.
best_facts.why_surprising: Printing could not keep up with the inflation that printing caused.

best_facts.fact: A 2009 ad campaign for The Zimbabwean newspaper was printed on real Zimbabwean banknotes, because it was cheaper to print on money than on paper. It won the Outdoor Grand Prix at Cannes.
best_facts.why_surprising: Money was the cheapest available paper.

best_facts.fact: In 2018 a Venezuelan artisan wove a handbag from 1,000 bolivar notes worth about 17 US cents at the exchange house, and sold it for about 13 dollars.
best_facts.why_surprising: As fibre, the money was worth about 75 times more than as money.

best_facts.fact: In 1923 the Bauhaus student Herbert Bayer designed emergency banknotes for the State of Thuringia. Worth almost nothing then, they are now museum pieces at the V&A.
best_facts.why_surprising: The most worthless money became some of the most valued design.

best_facts.fact: Venezuela cut 14 zeros from its currency between 2008 and 2021: one bolivar digital equals 100 trillion of the bolivars of 2007.
best_facts.why_surprising: A modern country lost more zeros than Weimar Germany did in 1923.

best_facts.fact: Venezuelans reported losing about 11 kg of body weight on average in 2017, according to a national survey by three universities.
Germany's famous 1923 hyperinflation ranks only fifth in the Hanke-Krus table; Hungary 1946, Zimbabwe 2008 and Yugoslavia 1994 were all faster.
best_facts.why_surprising: The textbook case is not the record holder.

best_facts.fact: In 1923 German restaurant bills could double while diners were eating, and pastors collected Sunday offerings in laundry baskets.
best_facts.why_surprising: Inflation fast enough to change a price between soup and dessert.

best_facts.fact: After Germany stabilised, the Nazis won just 2.6 percent of the vote in 1928. Their breakthrough came during the deflation and austerity of 1930 to 1933, not the hyperinflation.
best_facts.why_surprising: The popular story about Weimar has the timing wrong.

best_facts.fact: In 2008 Zimbabwe's capital stopped buying water treatment chemicals; a cholera epidemic followed that killed more than 4,000 people.
best_facts.why_surprising: A currency collapse can kill through the water pipes.

best_facts.fact: Nicolas Maduro, whose government had jailed currency traders, said of Venezuela's de facto dollarisation in 2019: 'Thank God it exists.'
best_facts.why_surprising: The man who blamed the dollar ended up praising it.

best_facts.fact: Zimbabwe's bearer cheques carried an expiry date, as if money could go off like milk.
best_facts.why_surprising: Even the state did not expect its money to last.

best_facts.fact: In 2014 Zimbabwe, with no currency of its own, approved the Indian rupee as one of nine foreign currencies for accounts and trade.
best_facts.why_surprising: India's money became, briefly, Zimbabwe's money too.

best_facts.fact: Keynes wrote in 1919 that 'Lenin is said to have declared' that the best way to destroy capitalism was to debauch the currency. Nobody has found Lenin saying it.
best_facts.why_surprising: One of the most quoted lines in economics rests on hearsay.

best_facts.fact: In January 2026 Zimbabwe recorded single-digit inflation in its own currency for the first time in almost 30 years.
best_facts.why_surprising: The home of the 100 trillion dollar note now has inflation lower than many rich countries had in 2022.

side_dish.title: Money illusion: why the number on the note fools us
side_dish.body_md:
In 1928 the Yale economist **Irving Fisher** published a small book called *The Money Illusion*. His point was simple: people think in the number printed on money, not in what it buys. A worker given a 10 percent raise in a year of 12 percent inflation often feels richer, though he is poorer.

In 1997 the psychologists Eldar Shafir and Amos Tversky, with the economist Peter Diamond, tested this with simple stories. Two people get the same real deal: one a 2 percent raise with no inflation, the other a 5 percent raise with 4 percent inflation. Most people judged the second one happier, even after agreeing the first was better off. The nominal number pulls at us.

Hyperinflation is where money illusion breaks. When prices double in a day, nobody can keep thinking in marks or bolivars. People switch, almost overnight, to a stable unit: dollars, rand, cigarettes, kilos of rice. Venezuelan market sellers in 2026 still price in bolivars, but buyers do the sums in dollars.

The illusion is strongest at low inflation, exactly where central banks like the RBI aim to keep us. That is one reason a stable 4 percent feels like nothing at all, and one reason why its slow effect on savings is so easy to ignore.

Try it: what was your salary, or your pocket money, ten years ago? Now ask what it would buy today.

offline_task.title: Live one day at 24.7 hours
offline_task.body_md:
**Ten minutes with a pen and today's grocery bill.**

1. Write down what you spent on food today, in rupees. Call it P.
2. Zimbabwe in November 2008: prices doubled about once a day (every 24.7 hours). Write P, 2P, 4P, 8P... for each day of one week. On day 7 the same food costs about 128 times as much. After 30 days it costs roughly half a billion times as much.
3. Weimar in October 1923: doubling every 3.7 days. Work out the price after 30 days (about 2 to the power 8, so about 270 times).
4. India at the RBI's 4 percent target: use the **rule of 70**. Divide 70 by the inflation rate to get the years for prices to double. 70 / 4 = about **17.5 years**.
5. Now look at the oldest banknote or coin you can find at home, or ask an older relative what a cup of tea, a cinema ticket or a bus fare cost when they were your age. Work out the yearly inflation that turns that price into today's.

**Notice**: at 4 percent the doubling takes half a generation, so we barely see it. At 50 percent a month it takes under two months. The mathematics is the same; only the speed changes.
